text:
alex: Heads-up — after the kernel selector rollout on 2026-03-02 we saw a noticeable drop in prefix cache hit-rate. dashboard shows hit_rate from ~87% -> ~62% for short prompts (<=64 tokens). p50 latency bumped ~18ms. anyone else tracking this?

priya: yeah saw the alert this morning. canary traces show KV cache lookups returning misses where the prefix is identical except for trailing spaces. iirc we introduced stricter prefix normalization in the tokenizer->keypath change. might be a keying mismatch.

dan: i rolled the quant-kernel path that week. kernel selection logic switches to fast-quant when avg_seq < 80. i didn't touch keying but the serialization changes to reduce memory copies could alter how we hash the key (ordering of fields). will double-check.

sasha: dropping a couple quick artifacts: small flamegraph from the canary (perf-bot link) and a sample trace showing a sequence of misses. gist: https://perf.company/redwood/kv-miss-20260302

perf-bot: nightly-regression-run completed: prewarm_hit_rate=0.65, production_hit_rate=0.62, cold_start_ratio=0.18. repro script attached.

alex: thanks. question — is this strictly a key mismatch (so older cached entries are effectively orphaned), or are we seeing lower reuse because batching heuristics changed (merge window shrank -> fewer shared prefixes per batch)? both would reduce hit-rate.

priya: good point. i sampled request batches: post-rollout we saw 30% fewer merges for concurrent small requests. the merge window was tightened to reduce tail latency for large sequences. that change likely reduced batch-local reuse.

dan: ok so two hypotheses: (A) key canonicalization change -> existing cache entries invalidated, (B) batching change -> lower local reuse. both plausible. which to triage first?

sasha: my vote is to instrument key hashes emitted at cache boundary and compare counts across canary vs prod. cheap and tells us if previous entries are still addressable. also capture merged_batch_size distribution.

alex: agreed. i'll add a temporary metric: kv_key_hex and kv_lookup_bucket (hit/miss) and tag with kernel_variant and batch_window_ms. quick dashboards should show correlation.

infra-bot: created ticket INF-879: "Investigate KV cache hit-rate regression after kernel & batching changes" and assigned to @dan @priya.

priya: while we instrument, we should also prototype warmup strategies. i sketched three options: deploy-time warmer (run across canary nodes at deploy), autoscale-triggered prefetch (on scale-up event, seed top-k prefixes), and scheduled background seeder (nightly low-rps sweep).

alex: add a fourth: on-demand synthetic microbursts — when a new instance comes up, emit a handful of synthetic requests that exercise most common prefixes. cheaper than full deploy-time sweep.

dan: costs: deploy-time warmer hits all instances during rollout -> immediate warm cache but high spike. autoscale-triggered seeds only when capacity grows -> lower cost but might still miss if traffic pattern shifts. scheduled seeder covers steady-state but not bursty growth. microbursts are attractive.

sasha: attached a tiny synthetic warmer script i used locally:
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# seed common prefixes into KV cache
for p in "hello" "summarize" "qa:" "translate:"; do
  curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood-internal/generate \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $SEED_TOKEN" \
    -d '{"model":"rwd-7b","input":"'$p' example","seed":42,"no_store":false}' &
  sleep 0.2
done
```

priya: nice. for on-demand we need idempotency and to avoid polluting quota/metrics. use a reserved seeding token and tag requests with header `X-Seeder: true` so we can exclude from cost analytics. also limit to top-100 prefixes from the workload profiler.

perf-bot: experiment suggestion: A/B compare deploy-time warmer vs microbursts for 24h on canary fleet. metrics: prewarm_hit_rate, end_to_end_p95, cold_start_ratio, cost_tokens_seeded.

alex: propose rollout plan: 1) instrument key hashes and merged_batch_size (48h), 2) run A/B microburst vs deploy-warmer on a small customer cohort (72h), 3) evaluate and pick winner, 4) implement autoscale-triggered seeding as fallback.

dan: i'll own instrumentation and the microburst harness. priya can own the seeder token + filtering. sasha can run the A/B dashboards and perf comparisons.

priya: question: if key canonicalization is the root cause we should also consider a migration step to canonicalize stored keys (or accept a warm-period and let traffic repopulate). migrating the KV store is risky. prefer detect+roll-forward first.

alex: agreed — no KV migration without a really strong case. quick mitigation: add a compatibility layer that accepts old-style keys for a short window (lookup both variants), then flip once warm. cheap and safe.

sasha: i can prototype dual-lookup in the runtime and feature-flag it. if we see hit-rate jump, we know it's keying.

infra-bot: INF-879 updated: milestones set, owner tags updated, ETA for instrument rollout = 2 days.

alex: cool. next steps: dan adds metrics + microburst harness, sasha prototypes dual-lookup flag, priya creates seeder token and top-k prefix list. we reconvene in #eng-runtime in 48h with dashboards. :thumbsup:
